div.p: This paper contributes to the emerging literature investigating agglomeration externalities in developing countries and focuses on the less studied differences between the formal and the informal sector. Using establishment-level data and instrumental variable estimations, we find that both formal and informal establishments benefit from agglomeration externalities. We provide evidence that informal establishment total factor productivity (TFP) increases more with city size than formal establishment TFP. We also provide causal evidence on the source of agglomeration externalities by formality status by examining industry coagglomeration pairs and instrumenting with data on Columbian input-output and labor industry-pair relationships. We find little evidence of benefits from stronger input-output relationships at the city level, but substantial benefits associated with shared labor.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: with informal entrepreneurs (Busso et al., 2012;Dabla-Norris & Feltenstein, 2005;Loayza, 1996;Sarte, 2000).

Almost nothing is known about the difference in the size of the agglomeration economies for formal and informal firms. This study contributes to the emergent literature on agglomeration externalities and informality by exploiting a unique dataset on the universe of formal and informal establishments in Peru. We use these data to estimate the change in establishment productivity as a function of city size and explore heterogeneous effects by formality status. We further investigate the sources of these externalities by examining whether the co-location of industry pairs in a certain city is explained by the labor-market interactions and input-output relationships of those industries in that location.

We estimate production functions in which total factor productivity (TFP) is a function of the agglomeration externalities captured by the population size. To measure informality, we use two proxies: the absence of tax-id and a measure of informal labor. We account for potential sources of endogeneity by instrumenting for the population with both geological variables and historical population. We also employ these instruments in a variant of the two-stage estimation method introduced by Combes et al. (2008). We demonstrate heterogeneous effects for formal and informal establishments, with informal establishments benefiting more from increases in population size.

Agglomeration externalities can be thought of as generating localized increasing returns to scale-decreasing average costs as output increases in the location. The "sources" of agglomeration were first discussed by Marshall (1920) and the literature generally refers to three Marshallian "sources": labor-market interactions, linkages between intermediate and final good suppliers, and knowledge spillovers. As noted by Duranton and Puga (2004), the Marshallian "sources" may be the result of underlying mechanisms that produce observationally equivalent outcomes. These mechanisms either directly affect productivity (technological externalities) or reduce the average costs of production (pecuniary externalities). More recently, Combes and Gobillon (2015) demonstrate the empirical challenge of distinguishing between the mechanisms (and further whether they are acting through changes to the technology or input costs). Our data are not well-suited to uncovering underlying mechanisms. Thus, we follow much of the empirical literature and focus on overall size and classic Marshallian "sources" of agglomeration economies. Our primary analysis concentrates on the change in productivity associated with city population. Our exploration of Marshallian sources focuses on labor market interactions and input-output relationships. Glaeser and Henderson (2017) note that the presence of a large informal sector is one of many reasons to suspect that the advantages and disadvantages of agglomeration will be different in the developing world. Combes and Gobillon (2015) review the nascent literature on agglomeration in developing world contexts recently. Most studies examine the relationship between some measure of productivity, most commonly wages, and some measure of the market size (city size, market potential, etc.) as the local determinant of agglomeration economies. The focus on wages as the productivity measure has advantages in the developing world context, but a number of confounding factors, such as housing prices, amenities, local monopsony power, and so forth, can affect wages.

Examining measures of productivity such as TFP avoids some of these issues (at the expense of creating new ones that we discuss later). Combes and Gobillon (2015) note only two studies of developing country TFP and a local determinant of agglomeration other than market size, both of which examine Chilean establishments and do not address the endogeneity of agglomeration measures. A more recent working paper by Guevara-Rosero et al. (2019) examines the effects of industry concentration, diversity, competition, and density on Ecuadorian establishments using production function estimates and generalized method of moment. The research herein helps fill the remaining gap with an empirical strategy that addresses multiple potential sources of endogeneity as well as using colocation patterns to investigate sources (rather than direct TFP estimates).

Only a handful of studies consider the informal sector when researching agglomeration economies in developing countries. Yet, the informal sector comprises a large portion of economic activity and the labor force in developing countries. Overman and Venables (2005) suggest theoretically ambiguous agglomeration effects associated with informality. They also indicate that we should not assume no agglomeration economies for the informal sector. Duranton (2016) highlights this issue when he notably includes wages paid by informal firms in his analysis of agglomeration in Colombia. His findings suggest higher returns to agglomeration in the informal sector. García (2019) similarly finds stronger elasticity of wages with respect to density for informal workers than formal workers in Colombia. In a recent working paper, Figueroa Gil (2018) uses Peruvian household-level data to analyze the effect of the population size on average wages per city and the type of workers. This author finds statistically significant positive agglomeration effects for informal workers but a small effect for formal ones. A similar result is shown by Tanaka and Hashiguchi (2020) who find that the density of local employment has a statistically significant positive effect on productivity in the informal sector, but a small effect in the formal sector. Mukim (2015) examines the co-agglomeration of formal and informal (unorganized) establishments in India, finding that establishment entry increases with interindustry linkages for both types but that own-industry externalities are only positively associated with informal births. This is consistent with the idea that informal firms are small and small firms benefit more from agglomeration externalities (Rosenthal & Strange, 2003, 2004). These studies suggest that formal and informal establishments differentially benefit from agglomeration externalities.
Section 3 discusses our empirical implementation in more detail.

In this section, we outline a conceptual framework for estimating the agglomeration effects within a production function framework. We begin with a traditional way to introduce agglomeration economies. Then, we differentiate between agglomeration economies for formal and informal establishments. Finally, we consider different sources of agglomeration externalities by studying the co-agglomeration of industries in our data. We highlight threats to the identification and describe how we address those with our empirical strategy.

div.head: | Two-step procedure
div.p: It is possible that estimates of agglomeration effects from (2) reflect unobserved productivity determinants that are correlated with input choices. We address this concern by implementing a variant of the two-step procedure developed by Combes et al. (2008) and instrumenting for population. 6 In the first stage, we estimate production functions with city and industry fixed effects, instead of the agglomeration measure. Specifically, we estimate:

div.p: Our parameter of interest β is the elasticity of average city TFP with respect to city size. As before, we estimate Equation (3) for the pooled sample as well as separately for formal and informal establishments. We also instrument for city population using either geological variables or historical population in our estimation of Equation (3). However, sorting can still bias our estimates in other ways not accounted for by the controls. To the extent that establishments that are more productive sort into larger cities, our estimates will overstate the elasticity of productivity with respect to city size. To the extent that less productive establishments sort into larger cities, our estimates will understate the elasticity.
To ascertain the robustness and sensitivity of our results, we also report results for five variants of this analysis.

First, we repeat the above exercise using establishments' average real wage of permanent workers as an alternative measure of productivity. We calculate average real wage using wages for permanent workers at each establishment divided by mean rents in the establishment's location. Second, we use an alternative definition of establishment informality based upon the presence of unpaid labor to define our samples of formal and informal establishments. Third, we exclude establishments from the Lima Metropolitan Area from the analysis to ensure that our results are not primarily driven by businesses in the prime city. Fourth, we use the Sivadasan (2009) method for implementing the Levinsohn and Petrin (2003) estimator to address potential concerns about endogenous input choices affecting our TFP estimates. Finally, we investigate the extent to which differential results by formality status are attributable to differences in the size of formal and informal establishments by repeating our estimates by formality and size.

div.head: | Coagglomeration
div.p: The geographic concentration of establishments within an industry is often taken as evidence of the existence of agglomeration externalities. Yet, establishments within industries share similarities along many dimensions and this makes it difficult to uncover the source of the agglomeration externalities causing such concentration. On the other hand, establishments in different industries tend to be more similar in some dimensions than others.

Establishments in industry-pairs can be expected to collocate based upon the potential for certain Marshallian externalities. By using the variation in the strength of labor-market interactions and input-output relationships across industry-pairs, we can, therefore, uncover the relative importance of the two sources of agglomeration externalities in the Peruvian context.

The CENEC data includes all industry sectors except for the sectors "agriculture and public administration and defense." It contains information on establishments' production, location, the four digit-International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) (fourth revision) industry, value-added, employment, expenses, tax payments, inventories, and so forth. In CENEC, the establishments are located in districts. In Peru, there are 1846 districts grouped in 195 provinces that correspond to 25 regions. However, our geographical unit is the city. Cities contain one or more neighbor districts. We use the list of cities with 20,000 habitants or more provided by INEI and apply the INEI's city-district correspondence to determine the location of the establishments.

To differentiate the effects between the formal and informal sectors, we require a working definition of informality. In our case, informality is defined as firms that produce legal goods or services but are not registered as a firm. Business registration is an objective criterion for classifying businesses as formal or informal that is commonly used in the literature (La Porta & Shleifer, 2014;Mukim, 2015;Schneider, 2005;Tanaka & Hashiguchi, 2020).

The extractive industries in k are metal ore mining, nonmetallic mineral ore mining and quarrying, and oil and gas extraction. Unskilled occupations k are defined as food preparation and serving-related occupations; building and grounds cleaning and maintenance occupations; construction and extraction occupations; installation, maintenance, and repair occupations; production occupations; and transportation and material moving occupations.

As noted in the informality literature, it is very difficult to have an unbiased indicator of informality because informal firms are often reluctant to report their legal situation to survey administrators. Studies on informality usually work with approximate measures of informality or focus only on labor informality. In our study, we take advantage of the fact that in the Peruvian census of firms, the establishments are asked their tax identification number, called Registro Único del Contribuyente (RUC). Registration in the National Superintendency of Tax Administration is a mandatory step to constitute a firm in Peru. Thus, we define informal firms as those firms that produce legal goods but do not provide their RUC when asked for it. 8 The RUC number is not a confidential number and it is provided to firms' customers in every sale receipt. One possible problem with this definition of informal firms is that firms could have provided a false RUC but this is a possible bias in all survey questions. If that is the case, the study underestimates the number of informal firms. The fact that it is well known that INEI does not provide establishment-level information to enforcement agencies reduces the potential severity of this issue in our data. Figueroa Gil (2018) uses the definition of labor formality but his results are in the spirit of ours, suggesting that our variable is capturing the effects of informality associated with quasi-legality or operating outside the regulatory and taxing system. Our definition is similar to the definition of formal and informal sectors used in studies of agglomeration economies in India, which define informal (manufacturing) firms as those that are not registered with the government (e.g., Mukim, 2015). The difference between our definition based on RUC and the Indian registration definition is that in India small firms are exempt from registration,foot_4 and, therefore, 93% of the informal firms in Mukim (2015) are small firms with less than five workers. However, the definitions share the basic distinction of legal status. For the sensitivity analysis, we also use a different definition of informality based on the number of unpaid employees in each firm.

div.head: | Summary statistics
div.p: The census took place in 2008 and the production questions correspond to the economic year 2007. The original census data is composed of 864,030 establishments. We discard establishments that did not provide 2007 production information. In 78% of these cases, the establishment started operations in 2008, and, therefore, did not have 2007 production. Observations reporting negative value-added and/or provided a negative capital value are dropped when we take logarithms. Finally, we restrict our sample to only those cities with 20,000 or more inhabitants according to INEI. Our resulting sample includes 380,864 establishments.
Table 1 shows the distribution of establishments in the final sample by major industry and formality status.

Approximately 62% of all sample establishments belong to the sector "trade, maintenance, and repair service of vehicles." The next biggest sectors are "lodging and restaurants," "other services," and "manufacturing."

Nearly all establishments in the "fishing and aquaculture" sector are informal establishments. The "trade, maintenance, and repair service of vehicles" sector has the second-highest share of establishments that did not report a tax-id at just over 36%. The sectors with the highest proportion of formal firms are "oil, mineral, and natural gas extraction," "financial services, insurance and pensions," and "construction."

div.head: | CHANGES IN PRODUCTIVITY WITH CITY SIZE
div.p: In Section 5.1, we establish that agglomeration effects exist in our developing world context and that these are large compared to those estimated for the developed world and some (but not all) emerging and developing economies. We also establish that there are heterogeneous benefits to agglomeration for formal and informal establishments. We repeat our TFP exercise using wages in Section 5.2. Section 5.3 presents some robustness and sensitivity analyses. labor's share in the production function (0.75), which yields a wage elasticity of 0.049. 12 Thus, our estimate is well within the range of estimates reported for the developed world of 3%-8% (Rosenthal & Strange, 2004) and is also in line with estimates for Brazil, India, Mexico, and Colombia (Ahrend et al., 2017;Chauvin et al., 2017;Combes & Gobillon, 2015;Duranton, 2016;Melo et al., 2009).

div.head: | Effect of agglomeration on establishment TFP
div.p: Our elasticity estimate increases slightly when we instrument for the population in Columns 2 and 3. The twostage procedure using the geological instruments (Column 4) yields a similar elasticity; although imprecisely estimated given the small sample and somewhat weak instruments. The estimate in Column 5 uses the two-stage procedure and the historical population instrument. The historical population is a much stronger instrument than the geological variables for the second-stage estimates. Column 5 indicates a stronger elasticity of approximately 0.074. Scaling this estimate by one over labor's share of production yields an elasticity of 0.11, which is generally larger than estimates for the developed world as well as some emerging economies estimates. However, Chauvin et al. ( 2017) and Combes and Gobillon (2015) report 10%-20% elasticities of wages with respect to city size for China and India. Thus, our estimates are not implausibly large. Rather, they suggest that establishments in less developed places may benefit substantially more from agglomeration economies.

The results from Table 4 also seem to indicate that agglomeration effects differ by city size. While the OLS and IV estimations in Columns 1-3 of Table 4 are at the establishments level, and, therefore, larger cities receive a higher weight in the estimation, the two-step procedure in Columns 4 and 5 is at the city level and small and large cities receive the same weight in the estimation. The higher results from the city level estimation provide evidence that smaller cities show higher agglomeration effects than larger cities. We will come back to this argument in Section 5.3.2 when we exclude the larger city Lima from the estimation.

Panels B and C of Table 4 report separate estimates for the samples of formal and informal establishments, respectively. Comparing the panels suggests that informal establishments benefit substantially more from agglomeration economies than formal establishments. Estimates between Panels B and C in each column are statistically different from each other. To assess the magnitude of the difference between estimates, we estimated a pooled data equivalent of separate regressions by formality status that includes an indicator for formality status and interacts every term with it (including the instruments). As seen in Table A5, this process consistently yielded a significant 0.02-0.04 greater TFP elasticity for informal establishments in Columns 1-3, whereas in the city-level estimations, the difference is significant but not statistically significant. We prefer the results from the separate regressions reported in Table 4, however, because we do not have a valid instrument for formality status, and, as indicated by the production parameter estimates in Table A5, formal and informal establishments clearly operate with different production parameters.

In Table 4, formal establishment estimates generally range from 0.02 to 0.06, while informal estimates range from 0.05 to 0.08. The larger agglomeration benefits for informal establishments are consistent with the evidence provided by Duranton (2016) using Colombian wages. Focusing on the estimates in Column 5, we estimate an elasticity of TFP with respect to city size of 0.06 for formal establishments and 0.08 for informal establishments. Multiplying by one over the estimate labor shares yields elasticities of 0.08 and 0.11 for formal and informal establishments, respectively.foot_7

div.head: | Definition of informality
div.p: Our definition of informality captures the legal status of the establishments. However, it is possible that some informal establishments falsely report a Tax ID number. While this definition is commonly used in the literature, labor studies sometimes apply a worker-based definition of informality. These studies use the lack of a formal labor contract to define a worker as informal. Our data does not include information on labor contracts; however, it does include information on unpaid labor at the establishment. Table A6 presents estimates using an alternative definition of informality based upon the presence of unpaid labor. Specifically, we reclassify any establishments that report employing unpaid labor as informal. The results are virtually unchanged.

div.head: | Excluding Lima
div.p: Table A7 reports the results of estimating our TFP specifications excluding the Lima Metropolitan Area. The City of Lima is the political and economic capital of Peru, hosting a large share of the country's overall economic activity.

The estimates for all establishments in Panel A of Table A7 are higher than those reported in Table 4, with the estimates in Column 5 indicating an elasticity of 0.11 (compared to 0.08 in Table 4). Panels B and C report the results separately for formal and informal establishments and confirm the heterogeneity by formality status documented thus far.

The higher agglomeration effects by excluding Lima indicate that Lima is "too large" and that its agglomeration effects might be negative or lower than the mean of the effects in the other cities of the country. This could be explained by a concave productivity-agglomeration relationship where Lima has reached the point where congestion effects, a characteristic of "primate cities" Combes et al. (2008), are too strong. This result is also in line with the higher agglomeration effects found once small and large cities are equally weighted using the city-level estimation of the two-step procedure (Columns 4 and 5 of Table 4).

div.head: | Levisohn-Petrin instruments
div.p: As discussed above, it is possible that our estimated TFP is biased due to the correlation between input choices and unobserved productivity. While the two-step procedure should alleviate some of this concern, we further investigate the issue by following the Levinsohn-Petrin methodology modified in Sivadasan (2009). The author adopts the methodology to the case of a repeated cross-sectional database and constructs instruments from location-industry-specific electricity expenditures in the previous year. In our case, we only have a crosssectional sample of establishments. Therefore, we need to take the instruments from another database, the A8. Our estimated elasticity of TFP with respect to city size is similar to our findings using OLS and IV estimations in Columns 1-3 of Table 4 for formal firms.

Although we cannot repeat this exercise for all our estimates, the fact that the Sivadasan-Levinsohn-Petrin estimate is in the range of our main results for formal firms (0.02-0.06, Table 4) provides some reassurance that the potential correlation between input choices and unobserved productivity is not driving our results in a meaningful way.

div.head: | Establishment size
div.p: Finally, Rosenthal and Strange (2003) find that small establishments are more dependent upon agglomeration externalities than large establishments. It is, therefore, possible that our findings of the differences in the effects of agglomeration externalities on formal and informal establishments are attributable to differences in their size-rather than by differences in legal status captured by our informality measure. Table A9 reports the results for pooled, formal, and informal establishments that are large (defined as 10 or more employees) in Panels A-C, respectively, and small (defined as less than 10 employees) in Panels D-F, respectively.

The first thing to note is that our estimates for large establishments contrast Rosenthal and Strange's findings-agglomeration externalities do appear to have an effect on the largest establishments in our sample.

Panel A indicates large establishment elasticities ranging from 0.06 to 0.13, which are stronger than those for small establishments in Panel D. These elasticities are mainly driven by the formal establishments (Panel B). Informal large establishments (Panel C) are less than 5% of the sample of large establishments and the agglomeration effects are not statistically significant. It should be noted that our definition of small and large differ from those employed by Rosenthal and Strange (2003) and other studies using developed country data. Our 10-employee threshold is much lower because of the substantially different distribution of employment in Peruvian establishments than in the U.S.

establishments. For example, the 99th percentile employment in our data is 13. Thus, most of our sample of "large" establishments would be defined as "small" using the U.S. cutoff values (e.g., Rosenthal and Strange classify establishments with fewer than 25 employees as small). Our findings of stronger agglomeration benefits for our "large" formal establishment may, therefore, suggest a nonlinear relationship between establishment size and agglomeration externalities, whereby benefits increase with employment until some point and begin to diminish thereafter. They also show evidence that informal firms benefit less from agglomeration externalities when they grow.

The estimates for small establishments are similar to those reported in Table 4, although generally less precisely estimated. The estimates in Panels E and F indicate elasticities ranging from 0.02 to 0.06 for small formal establishments and 0.05-0.08 for small informal establishments, respectively. These results suggest that the stronger estimated effects of city size for informal establishments are not an artifact of informal establishments being relatively small, and, therefore, benefitting more from agglomeration externalities. Instead, the relative strength is attributable to either differential benefits associated with formality status or to differential sorting of small establishments into formality status on the basis of productivity.

div.head: | SOURCES OF AGGLOMERATION EXTERNALITIES
div.p: Having established the existence of agglomeration externalities for Peruvian establishments as well as the heterogeneity in agglomeration benefits by formality status, we now investigate the sources of agglomeration. We follow best practices in the literature and do this by examining the extent to which establishments in industry-pairs collocate based upon similarities in labor and the strength of input-output relationships.

Table 6 presents the OLS and instrumented change in industry-pair coagglomeration as the occupations shared by the industries increases (Columns 1 and 4) and as the industries have closer customer-supplier relationships (Columns 2 and 5). Columns 3 and 6 consider both sources simultaneously while controlling for predicted coagglomeration from natural advantages. Panel A contains the results for coagglomeration of all establishments, while Panels B and C consider coagglomeration of formal and informal establishments, respectively.

We find that most of the documented agglomeration benefits are attributable to labor market interactions, with the estimated effect of the labor-market interaction variable much higher than that of the input-output variable. In the instrumented multivariate regression for all establishments (Panel A, Column 6), the effect of the labor-market interaction is 0.168 and statistically significant, while the effect of the input-output variable is small and not statistically distinguishable from zero. They report that labor-market interactions are much stronger for services but still find that input-output interactions are important.

To investigate whether our lack of input-output results is driven by differences in the sectoral composition of industry-pairs, we re-estimate Table 6 using only manufacturing industry-pairs. This exercise also yields an insignificant relationship between coagglomeration and input-output interactions for the pooled and formal samples. However, input-output interactions are a significant predictor of colocation of informal manufacturing industry-pairs. Diodato et al. (2018) demonstrate that input-output linkages have declined in importance over time in the U.S., but it seems unlikely that transportation and communication linkages in Peru are developed to the extent necessary to erase benefits from proximity to suppliers and customers. Peru's transportation infrastructure is in fact underdeveloped, and, therefore, the colocation of suppliers and final producers might be more visible at a smaller spatial scale. To investigate this issue further, we recalculate the coagglomeration index at the district-level (approximately equivalent to U.S. counties) and repeat the analysis from Table 6. Table 7 reports the results of this exercise.

Input-output linkages significantly predict district colocation of both formal and informal establishments, but estimates are small and generally around 0.01. Labor-market interactions are also a significant source of agglomeration benefits for district colocation; however, the estimated effect is smaller than our estimates for city coagglomeration. Diodato et al. (2018) also report labor-market interaction estimates that reduce with area size (state, city, and county), indicating that our findings are in line with the literature.

div.head: | CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper contributes to our limited understanding of agglomeration externalities in the developing world in a number of important ways. First, we document the existence and strength of agglomeration externalities in a Latin American country during a period of relative stability and prosperity. Although data limitations prevent using the state-of-the-art techniques for addressing sorting issues that may affect our estimates, our empirical strategy allows us to address the other potential sources of endogeneity and provides reasonable estimates of the agglomeration externalities.

Second, we exploit the unique nature of our data on the universe of formal and informal establishments in Peru to explore heterogeneous agglomeration benefits by formality status. We find that agglomeration economies are stronger for informal establishments, which is similar to Tanaka and Hashiguchi (2020) and Duranton (2016).

These results are robust to the definition of formality and are not attributable to differences in establishment size between formal and informal businesses. These results suggest the need for additional research into productivity effects in markets characterized by large informal sectors with low entry costs and low operating costs that do not result from higher productivity.

Finally, we provide causal estimates of the potential source of agglomeration externalities in Peru by estimating the effect of labor-market interactions, input-output relationships, and natural advantages on the coagglomeration of industry pairs using instruments constructed from Colombian data and predicted colocation due to natural advantages. We find that the primary source of agglomeration benefits in the city is labor market interactions. Given that most value-added production in our study is labor-intensive, it may not be surprising that most of the externalities occur through labor-market interactions. This suggests that there may be substantial productivity benefits from policies aimed at improving overall skill levels in the labor market.

figure.figDesc: DataThe research uses confidential microdata from the 2007 National Economic Census (CENEC) as its primary data source. The CENEC provides a unique data source for investigating differences in agglomeration externalities for formal and informal establishments. We also use the 2006 Annual Economic Survey, the 1981 National Census of Population and Households, the 2007 National Household Survey (2007 Encuesta Nacional de Hogares [ENAHO]), and the 2007 Peruvian input-output matrix, to calculate the Levinsohn-Petrin estimator, the historical population instrument and the labor-market interaction variable and the input-output variable for the coagglomeration analysis, respectively. All these databases were provided by the Peruvian National Statistical Institute (Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática, INEI). We also use the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission digital elevation

ISIC and the Peruvian economic activity code provided by the Peruvian Ministry of Finance, resulting in 92 industry groups. To build the IVs, we use the Colombian 2005 input-output matrix and the 2007 Integrated Household Survey (Gran Encuesta Integrada de Hogares 2007) provided by the Colombian National Statistic Department (Departamento Administrativo Nacional de Estadística). To relate industries in Peru and Colombia, we regroup industries to form a mapping of 47 industries. Since CENEC excludes sectors "agriculture and public administration and defense," we ended up working with 43 industries.
